<reason>Both sides argued cleanly and stayed on-topic, but A built a more coherent throughline: platforms already traffic in the same "third-party" graph data internally (display, mutual-friend suggestions, address-book import), so the accountability-boundary objection applies asymmetrically only at the point of exit. B's strongest asset — the CA analogy and the registry/liability dilemma — was pressed hard in Pressure Questions, but A's answer (liability falls on the receiving party, analogous to existing API abuse enforcement, with the exporter authenticating registered destinations the way it already authenticates growth partners) directly answered the mechanism question CON demanded. CON's closing repeats that "growth partners are chosen, not owed by law" — a fair point, but it doesn't fully rebut A's core reductio that platforms already export similar relational data across boundaries when it serves their own growth, undermining the principled non-transferability claim. B's insistence that a self-export "souvenir" is the only acceptable remedy under GDPR-style rules effectively conceded that CON's proposed alternative doesn't solve the lock-in problem A raised from the outset (exit without orphaning your audience), and A capitalized on this concession clearly in Rebuttal 2 and Closing. The debate stayed tightly focused on this liability/accountability crux, and A's closing sharpened the tradeoff (moat restated as consent) more memorably than B's dilemma framing, which mostly reasserted earlier claims without fully closing the gap on why authenticated scoped transfer inevitably fails.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's response to the Cambridge Analytica analogy — reframing it as a covert access-control failure rather than an authenticated, consented, purpose-limited transfer — combined with the Pressure Questions exchange about why platforms may already display/import graph data for their own growth but not let users port the same visible tie, was the most decisive clash. B's rebuttal to this (accountability boundary argument) was intellectually serious but ultimately didn't fully defeat the internal-inconsistency charge A pressed twice.</best_rebuttal>
